Q12 Is it fair game for sketch writers to comment on appearance — perhaps nail varnish colour ?

N ot being a sketch writer , it is very hard for me to comment on how they weigh up what they a re going to include in a sketch. One would hope that their main focus is going to be t he narrative and the discussion that they a re focusing on. But I would imagine that there are moments whe n they sometimes want to talk about th ese colourful characters who occupy our world, in order to show people that it i s not monochrome out there ; that there are women, men , colourful characters . They will use descriptions of what people are wearing in order to do that . But , as I say , that is different from how we as news journalists approach things , so perhaps it would be useful for your C ommitte e to ask one of the sketch writers to come and talk to you about how they make their judgments, because it i s not something I have ever been very good at , and nor is it something I would ever want to do.

Q13 Good afternoon , panel. My first question is a bout the Women’s Lobby , which has been in its current iteration for nearly seven years . I just want to know , from your point of view , how ethnically diverse it is . If it is not diverse , what more needs to be done to increase representation ? I wi ll start with Caroline first, please.

That is a really good question , and actually it is something we a re very conscious of. We had discussions about this only last week, and i t i s not just ethnicity that we a re interested in terms of diversity ; it is a lso about access . W e still have a Lobby that is predominantly privately educated , Oxbridge journalists, which is reflected in the Women’s Lobby , b ut we do n o t have a very ethnically diverse Lobby in general, or Women’s Lobby e ither . W e want to improve access on all levels , because one of the reasons we set up the Women’s Lobby is that , having come into this world nearly 20 years ago now , I can remember how daunting and completely intimidating it was to come here and having the most terrible feeling of imposter syndrome. O ne of the main impetus es of the Women’s Lobby is to try and create a supportive network for women of all backgrounds and ethnic diversity to come into and to be able to take part and work in the Lobby .

W e are going to be holding a number of events that look specifically at access, because that is something that we are very much aware of which has n o t been given enough focus as yet. But we still have a major problem in terms of just equality , a nd the ratio of male to female journalists here is still 2 :1 at best. In some papers there are still all - male teams . In the heyday w e had seven female political editors , but we ha ve subsequently lost two of them , a nd of course Pippa is moving on. Al though Heather i s gone , we a re not replacing like for like unless The M irror gets a new female political editor , so w e are still striving on all fronts to make sure that the Lobby is as equal as it possibly can be , b ut we face challenges on every front, right from representation of women to men right through to access and diversity.

T hank you very much for asking the question. Making sure that we reflect our audiences is really important, not just moral ly but also from a sheer business point of view—w omen are 50% of the population. The y a re our audience , they are our people , and people from different backgrounds , so we n eed to make sure that we are catering for everybody.

We ha ve a target at the whole of S ky , including Sky News, o f increasing our ethnic make - up of people to 20% by 2025 , which is a long way to go. I do n o t ever want to employ somebody because of the colour of their skin , as that should never come into it. I a m very proud that we have Mhari Aurora from News UK com ing to join us as a political correspondent, which is great. Faisal was our p olitical e ditor before Beth , of course, so we are very committed to making sure we are reflecting people from all backgrounds, whether it i s different social backgrounds, gender or ethnicity. But this is something that the industry recognises i t still needs to work hard on .

Just to add to that , similar to Sky , the BBC actually has a firm target of reaching 20% of ethnic diversity over the next three to five years , alongside the 50 : 50 commitment on male and female employment and the 12% target of disabled employe e s. A lso , a s Cristina says, it i s really about reflecting the audience, and we take soc io economic background as a really important target as well.
Q14 What role and responsibility do you think the media has in making politics a place that women want and can be in ? Cristina .

Great question. At the end of the day , our job is to report what goes on , not necessarily to shape policy or shape society. We can reflect society, but our job is to report the news , not to shape it. H aving more women in senior positions, which is something I a m personally really passionate about , ensures that there is a range of voices at the table when it comes to making decisions. In terms of our employees who work in politics , I have never had anyone come to me with any p articular —

I am s orry , but I a m going to have to suspend the meeting for a D ivision in the H ouse. Apologies. We a ll have to go and vote apart from me , because I c haired the Public Bill C ommittee when this Bill was in Committee .
Sitting suspended for a Division in the House.
On resuming—

As I was saying, we can only report what goes on in politics and in this country. How women make politics work as a profession for them is obviously a question for female politicians , but I do accept that it is a tough environment for women. I can imagine it makes life quite hard , in terms of the hours and so on . I n terms of the way that women are treated , I work for a news organisation that I strongly believe does treat women fairly and does n o t describe them in a different way from male colleagues. But I accept that it must be a tough profession to be in .

Thanks , Cristina . Yes , it can be quite toxic , and y ou mentioned before about reporting of women. We know how Tracy Brabin was treated when she de ign ed to come into the C hamber wearing a n off-the- shoulder dress and how the media took that and blew i t up, b ut it did raise some money for charities, which was a positive thing. Katy , d o you want me to read the question out again ?
Yes please.
Q15 What role and responsibility do you think the media has in making politics a place that women can and want to be in?

Okay, I a m actually going to answer this from an audience perspective , because there are two ways to look at this . I a m happy to go back to the broader sense of it , b ut one of the things to consider when thinking about our coverage is this. I always describe our political reporting in two sections. One is what I would call kind of Green Bench , so it is the straightforward political knock about , the serious end of party politics , and then there i s the policy end . What I have tried to do during my time at Westminster is really think about ways that we can get to the policy end, which I think connects to women m uch more , which go es back to what we were talking about previously in terms of women having perhaps a different kind of eyesight on stories , and particularly politics.

We have made quite a lot of changes not only just at the BBC but with colleagues at this table around approaching stories that are policy - based , and actually writing them in a much more accessible manner so that women are more likely to read and l isten to them, turn them up . B ecause in the end, politics is about people and what matters to people and to our audience, and that i s a really important line to connect.

I would agree broadly with what everyone is saying . F or us , i t does n o t affect how we treat news —news is news , and w e are here to report what i s happening here , the policy debates and the knockabouts and all of those things. O ne of the things that N ews UK is very passionate about th at we a re using very much to our own advantage, and the broadcast side also have similar metrics , is that we use data a lot more to tell us about who our audiences are and what they a re interested in.

We know what our dwell times are , so we can look at a piece and see who is looking at it, whether it is women or men, and how long they are spending looking at which article, which does help us to reflect how we treat our content. For example, one of the things we do a lot more of now is long form. I nstead of doing a short, pithy news piece , we wi ll put up the read instead , because actually we find the audience e ngagement is better for longer - form bits of journalism about those often political, big, meaty subjects, which is why Tim Shipman's read ha s become a staple of T he Sunday Times , and which we find our audiences want more of.

A s much as we can , we try to be responsive to our audience , a nd virtually every day we get emails telling us what our women readers are reading most of , in order to make sure that we keep that at the forefront of our minds . A t the end of the day , we are only here to serve the people who are reading our website and our news , and indeed listening to the radio and television programmes that we make. It definitely is a key priority for everybody at News UK and is something that people are mindful of on a daily if not hourly basis.
Q16 Tha nk s , Caroline . Katy, w hy do you think the media , or parts of the media , represent women in such a different way from male politicians?

I am not sure that I agree with the concept of the question , a ctually . I know what you mean, b ut as a broadcaster I try to see no difference. That i s not to say that I a m blind to the difference , of course, particularly being a woman , but , a s we touched on before, when we come to reporting our politics , d o we treat the stories differently? We really should not do that , because in the end it is not really about the person’s gender ; it is about the politics and what is being done about it.

I think t he same r eally . I can only speak for where I work and we do n o t treat men and women any differently in terms of reporting on our political news or any news , f rankly . We and the BBC are both regulated by Ofcom , which can be quite a protection against anyone wanting to do that anyway.

Tha t does sometimes happen in the wider press , b ut we were just talking earlier about the por trayal of women and MPs and what they a re wearing. S ome sketch writers sometimes have quite a good go at some of the men about their appearance, but obviously in a more jovial way than they might with women , b ut at S ky N ews it is just not part of our reporting , I a m proud to say .

It should not be treated any differently , b ut there are issues where you do want to have more female voices in them . F or example , there are often stories . I can think of one recently around what ha s been happening in Downing Street , a nd there have been some complaints from young women who feel they have been treated disproportionately harshly compared with their male colleagues . I n the reporting of those stories, it i s actually important that you talk to more of the women involved than necessarily the men , i f you a re trying to make sure you move your argument along .

I n some of the stories that we ha ve covered recently regarding the sexual misconduct scandal , a large group of women were brought together with the Chief Whip to talk about the issue . It would have been silly for us to look at gender balance, for example, in doing that particular story, because of course it was the women who were involved in that meeting. While we do try and balance our reporting and make sure that if we are looking at particular issues , we speak to both m ale and female MPs so that there is gender balancing in our copy , t here are times when it i s inappropriate to do so , and obviously for the narrative reasons we do that.
Thank you for those responses to my questions , panel.
Bell, d o you have a follow - up question on that se ct ion?

Q17 Yes . The Committee o n Standards in Public Life published a report in 2017 on the abuse and intimidation experience d by parliamentary candidates. The report concluded that “ P rint and broadcast media also contribute to a culture in which elected public officials can become targets of threats and abuse. ”

That same year, another study found that Diane Abbott, the first black woman elected to P arliament, received more than half of all of the abuse aimed at female politicians online g enerally . I work ed for Diane for a number of years, and we would actually receive most of the death threats and abuse by email and post following the publication of certain headlines. T hese headlines were often worded incorrectly, and w e would even be able to challenge outlets to say that they should change them. But by then it was already out , o r if it was something on TV, it had already been a ire d .
I want to ask, w hat role , if any , d o you think your respective news outlets can play in the abuse of elected officials, in particular b lack women? We will start with Caroline .

A lot of those decisions are taken above my pay grade , as it were . Headlines and t he treatment of stories , in particular, is something that gets done by sub - editors, editors and deputy editors . But I do n o t shy away from your question , in that it is incumbent on all of us to think about that . I have been here for long enough to have seen friends and colleagues experience the kind of abuse that you a re talking about , and it i s not something that us as female journalists are immune to either.

W e do need to think about content very seriously . I will give you one way in which we can do that. We did think about this very carefully with the treatment of Nusra t Ghani when she came to us earlier this year to talk about her own experiences of what she perceived to be racism within the ministerial ranks, when she effectively said that she had been sacked a s a junior Minister for being “ t oo M uslim ” . S he was very concerned about the way in which we would treat that particular story , because she thought it would be a lightning rod for abuse. S he has a young family a nd obviously Twitter can be a particularly horrible place for women , and particularly for women from an ethnic minority background .

W e talked to her extensively about how she would like us to do the story, and one of the things she said was that she did n o t want a photograph of herself on the front page, which we adhere d to , as she thought that would make her more of a target. We also talked to her about whether or not we would have comments online . Obviously , we can turn comments off stories, a s those can often be particularly upsetting and give rise to further debate on social media, for example.

It is important for both us and you as politicians to be aware that there are tools at our disposal that can help limit and mitigate those kind s of things , b ut also do n o t be afraid to complain. I take on board what you say very seriously , but often it i s too late by the time that something has come to attention. I am very rarely off duty ; I get phone calls very late into the night and often through out Saturday night and early in the morning . I f somebody comes to me and says, “ Look, there is a genuine problem here that we could fix quite easily, which has just become a kind of lightning rod , p lease can you change it? ”, I would always run that past my line manager and on-call team very quickly and make sure that any changes were done to rectify that. I t is important to us and, certainly working in this industry, it is something that I and the rest of the team are pretty alive to these days.

I would just like to a nswer in general terms if it is okay , because I a m not sure o f the specific points you a re talking about . T he first thing is to say that you really want to get it right in the first place. A s you say, we absolutely str ive every day, hour and minute to write s omething that is correct , a nd we think about that very seriously , quite rightly of course.

As Caroline says, in terms of any complaints , there are very clear complaint rules and guidelines for the BBC. Likewise, if mistakes are made, then we endeavour to correct them very quickly indeed. I n my former role , as you were late at night, I was very early, so my phone would start at 6 am , a nd if there was an issue then you woul d consider it. Sometimes you would disagree, and that i s obviously the right thing to do a s an independent broadcast er . But if there was a mistake, then the key was to swiftly look at that.

W e have similar procedures in place to deal with complaints, but I think you a re probably not talk ing so much about complaints per se , but more abuse that arises from coverage. I and my senior editorial colleagues are very mindful when reporting on a story o f what the effect of that might be. Sometimes we can help mitigate against that , and at o ther times we can no t . Obviously, we can no t control what i s said on social media.

I would like to reiterate my personal view that nobody should suffer any kind of abuse — racist, sexist or anything “ is t ” — as part of their job. Sadly, women seem to be a bit of a soft target amongst the anonymous people on the Twittersphere. But , as I said, we spend a lot of time making sure that what we a re doing does n o t encourage any of that. W hen there are serious issues that people come up and talk about , we do report them , and maybe being open about the abuse one i s getting can actually sometimes show a light to society and say, “ This isn ’ t on . ”

I f I may just add to that , your point about online abuse is really key . I f you think about the last few years, certainly when I joined Westminster in 2014 , it just exploded really, a nd we ha ve been through this extraordinary arc . T he noise outside this place was reflected by the noise online , which for me has really made the connection very difficult.

Q18 Cristin a , you made a point about being a target following online abuse, but what about when it perhaps gets to a point when a woman in public life may feel she i s a target of the media ? I wi ll use the same example of Diane Abbott , when for a week or two during that particular election the media as a whole — p rint and broadcast — focused specifically on her making a mistake with a number. During that same election it was pointed out that a number of other politicians made mistakes, and none of them w as given the same level of coverage. T he excuse given for that was that this was more of a story. H ow can it be right , a nd , when politicians are doing the same thing , how do you usually judge w hether or not you focus on one more than the other, especially when it appears that women are targeted more in a certain way ?

I cannot remember the exact specifics of that . I remember the story , b ut I cannot remember where I was working at the time , to tell you the truth. At the end of the day , we are committed to being impartial and fair. Fairness is very important to me personally and also to our news organisation . If I feel that we are going down a route that is n o t fair, then I would be very vocal about that and challenge it.

A s I said, we a re regulated by Ofcom and complaints can be made , and I am not aware of any complaints upheld by Ofcom, certainly in the time that I ha ve been at S ky N ews. F airness is kind of ingrained in where I work, but whether it is i n other news organisations I cannot really comment .

I have a very similar answer . We just strive to look out for any imbalance in our reporting. We will always start the day with following our standards , which are impartial and balanced reporting in the public interest .

Exactly the same thing, really . We also have e ditorial standards and a system whereby people can report articles that they a re not happy with . N o journalist that I know welcomes those complaints w hen they come in . They are treated extremely seriously , and within a news organisation i t can be reputational ly damaging for that particular journalist to become the target of multiple complaints. I genuinely believe that most journalists I a m aware of, certainly within our news organisation and definitely within my team , would always be mindful of that.

On e of the steps and processes , in terms of looking at a story and working out whether or not you a re going to run it in the first place , would be asking yourself, “Is this going to attract a complaint for any of the reasons that we were set out, whether fairness, balance or accuracy ?” A s a journalist you should be asking yourself those questions every time you commit any article to paper , no matter what it is.

Q19 All of you allow comments in your online news pages. Do you have any set threshold for the level of abuse and comments , vitriol that is spewed at w hoever the subject of the article is , before you wi ll turn them off ? I wi ll start with Caroline.
Yes , we do . A ll of our comments are moderated, and so we do —
In advance?

Well, w e do have a certain system , s o if we see a particular story that we think is likely to attract people, there are certain subject areas that can be very volatile for our audiences . For example , discussions a bout transgender issues typically attract a lot of debate . T here is a kind of media plan thought of in advance about publishing a story . W e do n o t shy away from publishing those stories, particularly when they are in the public interest, which is the overriding reason that we publish stories in the first place. But yes, there is always a media plan about whether or not you have moderated, whether you have pre - moderated and indeed whether you have comments at all.

T here are articles that you wi ll see on the Times online website where there are n o comments allowed whatsoever. The other thing that we are encouraged to do is to moderate ourselves , and there are certainly journalists I know that will be sitting there looking at their own stories for many hours a day, and if they see something that they think reaches that threshold, they will s elf - police and report it to the building themselves , and also will intervene in debates to try and calm things down or moderate.

But in answer to your question, yes, there is both a media plan and also there are journalists who are so diligent in making sure that this does n o t become an issue that they police their own stories.

On the digital , I a m not aware that we have comments actually, but I wi ll double - check that and come back to you , because that i s not within my current remit. I can talk about the obviously wide - ranging scale of programmes , where if any abuse comes in from audience members or phone - ins for example, which is a radio version, then absolutely there are procedures for whether you a re going to put someone on air , a nd of course the presenters and editors are trained in what to do if people go over the top.

I am pretty certain that we do n o t have comments on our website, but I will double - check that for you . Picking up on what Katy said, we often do have panels of people and shows with audiences, and it is a very important job of the person presenting that show to make sure comments that are wildly off - beam are picked up on. But I believe a decision was made to turn off comments a while before I joined at Sky, because obviously it is something you do not have as much control over a s the words that you put out yourselves.

Q20 Before I go on to my questions about the Lobby , I just want to ask Katy something. You set off a whole train of thought in my mind when you referred to the Green Bench side of politics and the policy end, and you said that women tend to get more engaged with the policy end of it . That leads me to ask a kind of philosophical question, because the whole rules of the game at Westminster are basically written around the behaviours of men. They are combative , and increasingly I find myself sitting at Prime Minister’s questions thinking, “God, this is awful . ” Just as an aside , I wonder whether you have done any analysis of whether women are turned off by that side of politics, and to what extent?

Yes , we have. Caroline mentioned some of the data that The Sunday Times use s . As I am sure you are aware, the BBC has very developed data on audiences, which in relative terms is fairly new , really quite sophisticated and very useful as tools to look at where you are attracting and not attracting some areas of the audience. Yes, we have metrics on that, and there is research to show, if I can put it this way, that the more heat in the Chamber is not something that women are necessarily attracted to. I do not know that I should talk for all women, because actually I quite enjoy watching it myself, but I think there is a sense of the noise, and that perhaps the sometimes more shouty nature of the Chamber does put women off.

But I also meant in my answer that actually I do think there i s a responsibility, and the BBC has done this for many years, as we all have , b ut there is a responsibility to say, “ Hang on a minute , h ave you realised that everything is political? ”, so w hen you take your child to your primary school or you go to your GP, that is actually politics. W hen I talk to people and friends or family who say, “Oh well, I ’ m not really that interested in politics , ” I always say, “Well, e verything is political, and that ’ s wh y you should care, because it is about your life . ”

Q21 Manufactured heat is a turn - off, but I a m always struck , and colleagues will endorse this, that every time we go out knocking on doors , s omeone will always say, “ Why can ’ t you all work together? ” , to which I always say, “ Well, actually, we do . ” But there is no sexiness in the reporting of those sorts of things really, is there?

Well, we do have stories when there are successful alliances . I can think of a few that we ha ve done over the years when there are successes . A ctually, to go back to my point about policy , because it i s really good and we should go out of our way to say “ Actually, there ha s been an alliance here . ” T he shout y end of it — we all know what we a re talking about here — the PMQ s , the Brexit debate ; it i s the high end of drama . Y ou wi ll know more about this than me , b ut it feels to me that although it i s very loud, actually it i s a fairly small percentage of what you guys really do.

Q22 Ye s , the drama actually is a small part, but it i s increasingly what people see , and actually those who are interested in delivering good outcomes , we can stand up in the House of Commons and n o one pays a blind bit of attention to what we a re saying , b ut there we are — we digress.

Caroline , talking about the parliamentary Lobby specifically, d o you think that having a parliamentary p ass confers particular responsibilities on journalists in terms of how they report what goes on here?

Yes, there are very obvious responsibilities that come with having a p ass , and that can be demonstrated by the fact that there have been journalists who have lost their p asses, and we know that that has happened relatively recently. W e all work together in a space where we interact with each other in social spaces, for example, and I a m sure there are often temptations for journalists to take pictures of MPs behaving inappropriately , potentially on the Terrace . But we are very definitely told that that is something that we a re not allowed to do , and we do n o t do it.

But we do have a Lobby system whereby we have a relationship with the Commons authorities , who have frank conversations with the Lobby about what is and what is n o t acceptable in terms of our conduct on the Estate . But in terms of editorial guidelines , it is not something that would be welcomed — that there would be stipulations on what can or cannot be written about in terms of what goes on here and policies, because we do have a free press and we are regulated by our professional standards . It is really those professional standards that have to be held across all journalists, no matter where they work, that we adhere to.

Yes , there are certain things that we adhere to because it i s about where we work and the very particular nature of where we work , hence the example of photographs . But if you a re asking whether there should be rules about what we a re allowed to report , which of course there are around national security , and we g o t emails from Black Rod saying , “ Y ou can't report X , Y, Z ” w hen there was a terrorist attack in the vicinity , for example . W e were all very mindful that we were n o t going to do anything that was going to endanger life.

But if you a re talking more generally about whether or not we should be reporting the types of things that we ha ve referred to, for sketch writers and so on , th ose professional standards and conduct guidelines that we already have should really be the catch-all that basically make s sure that journalists uphold all of those very key principles that we ha ve referred to many times today, such as making sure that reporting is fair, accurate and balanced, and also that we are subject to a complaints process anybody is able to use.

Q23 In terms of conduct within the e state , there are very clear obligations that are imposed by the House authorities. But actually , the content is very much an editorial matter. But in terms of the organisations that have access to the Lobby , we have here three very professional ones with very high standards, but that is n o t true o f all the organisations that have access to the Lobby .

T hey are all covered . I can no t think of an organisation that i s not covered by those professional standards . Whether it be Ofcom or IPSO, we have the same coverage. Whether or not they uphold those professional standards is very much something that those organisations need to be overseeing . W here an organisation is found wanting , that needs to be challenged through the complaints processes, which is what it i s there for .

Q24 Do you think that , by and large , members of the Lobby do maintain a high degree of professional standard s ? I ask that question really because I think probably a lot of the more tittle - tattley abusive pieces are n o t necessarily always from people from the Lobby . Have you a ny observations on that?

It i s difficult to comment on other people ’ s behaviour , really. I know what my standards are here , and I am very much aware that I have a parliamentary p ass , which is my meal ticket , b asically — without it I can no t do my job. Therefore , I am very mindful of making sure that I do no t abuse the privileges that are given to me . T he Lobby system is a reminder of how we behave , and w e do talk to colleagues about our professional conduct, and nobody would want to be the journalist who breaks the embargo or breaks the confidential email that comes from House of Common security , for example.

If you a re asking me more broadly about professional conduct, most journalists are mindful of the professional standards that are required of them . W here they do n o t adhere to them, many of them are pulled up pretty quickly for it , i n my own personal experience . I ha ve seen that happen when complaints have been made , and the consequences of them . Not just as a Lobby correspondent, but as a journalist per se , broadly speaking what I have witnessed shows me that the system we have works, by and large. A s in every walk of life there is going to be the occasional bad a pple , or somebody that does n o t quite understand what i s required of them , b ut in my experience that ha s been a very rare occurrence.

Q25 Do members of the Lobby respect that this is a very privileged position? Because now we have so many channels of communication and so on, and this place is fairly accessible , t he Lobby was born from a time when this place did n o t like anyone reporting anything , and t herefore it was all tightly control led . Now we can not get enough PR , can we? But we still have this Lobby system . H ow would members of the Lobby f eel if we suddenly decided — perhaps we could recommend from this Committee , Madam Chairman — that actually the Lobby should be rescinded?

Well, t hat did happen . Dominic Cummings — the P rime M inister ’ s c hief adviser, as was — did try to effectively dismantle the Lobby system , and equally there was an attempt to prioritise outlets that were going to be more favourable towards reporting the actions of the G overnment. A woman, you see.

Of course, b ut a princip led stand was made to s ay, “ Actually no, we do value this system and access is important to us . ” In my view , it is still an extremely privileged role to hold , and one that everybody who gets that opportunity would be proud to hold. O n that basis , people are mindful of their behaviour , because they do not want to lose that access .

Q26 It is part of the pattern of accountability , i f you like , that we have a properly functioning system , which of course requires everyone to behave. I n terms of becoming part of the Lobby , to what extent do your news organisations train people to do that ? W hat i s the process for achieving that Lobby status?

For me it was largely being thrown in at the deep end . Carol yn will know this because I started my life as the Swansea Evening Post l obby c orrespondent , with absolutely no experience of covering politics , other than the fact that I had desperately wanted to do it and had taken an interest in politics. It is still very much about learning your trade on the job, and generally people who want to come into the Lobby used to come through a regional paper. There used to be a lot of people who came through the regional routes, which was actually really good for women because there were a lot more women on regional papers at the time.

There are a countless number of other women . Kitty Donaldson, another one of the female political editor s, was in it . We had a regional Lobby where we all bounced off each other and learn t the tricks of the trade , as it were.

I do n o t think anything ha s radically changed since then , e ven those people coming in from the nationals. It is something where you hit the ground and you start learning. A s a Lobby correspondent of course the most important tool is your contacts , and you cannot make contacts without really being here in the same way. I cannot point to any particular training courses that you would do , other than local government and central Government courses , which you do as part of your NCTJ exams , which i s it is pretty much how it begins.
Q27 That i s interesting though , because I would suggest that perhaps there is less of an old - boy network and public schools in the regional media than there is the national .

Which is why we had more women. B ut nobody tells you how to do it , and t hat adds to the kind of imposter syndrome when you get here really, because it is absolutely terrifying. I can remember arriving here and spending at least the first year c ompletely exhausted, shattered, bemused, bewildered, terrified, scared, and slowly but surely it ha s improved .
Q28 Ye s , you never stop being scared and exhausted though . The Lobby p ass is given to the organisation , rather than the individual , i s that correct?

There i s an allocation given to the organisation and those allocations go up and down depending on various factors. For example , there i s more digital presence here now, so a lot of the past allocations have gone up recently. But The Sunday Times ha s four passes, I believe, and those have been held predominantly by people in the Lobby , b ut occasionally a deputy editor has held one , or somebody else who wa s writing columns and feels they need access here . B ut it all goes through the standard processes , s o it is a decision for Black Rod , and we go through exactly the same vetting process as MPs i n order to get that pass .
Q29 Katy, how do you decide who becomes part of the Lobby for the BBC?

I hold this very proudly and I want to say the word democracy back to you if you a re talking about closing the Lobby . T hat would cause great concern , because I genuinely think that if you want to get a fair representation of what you do in this place, we absolutely need access to the H ouses. It c ould n o t be more important that I , or really m y r e porting t eam , come and see you and talk to you and really understand the story , as well as get stories, so we can talk to our audiences .
I n terms of the allocation , it is very similar to what Caroline says . We will have a number , a nd in my role in Westminster I ha ve to hand them out, which makes me very popular.
I was going to say, you have power.
Or un popular, yes.
Q30 What informs your thought process as you are handing them out?

A couple of things. T here are the primary people who are on air who are going to have to have them . T hen , in the practical sense , our producers who are going to news gather , come into this place , do the pictures and make things happen for TV , radio and online. F or me, I have one so that I can meet people who have concerns about the BBC or want to raise particular issues and talk about our coverage o verall .

I am jealou s, because I do not have one . It is only on an occasion like this that I get the chance to actually meet you all, or on social occasions. I have to admit, I do no t really know how the p asses are allocated at Sky. I am sure that , as with all the other organisations, we have a set number , and we give them to people who need them. But it i s really interesting , you talked earlier about politics being so much more than the bear pit of PMQ s. I remember the first time coming here to this H ouse a s a politics student and being actually quite shocked by the confrontational nature of it and the noise. If we want to show Britain and the world what goes on in politics, then Lobby p asses are needed to make sure that we a re reporting what i s going on in this H ouse and n ot just what the cameras are showing in PMQs .

Yes, because actually you could do an interesting piece to camera about some of the issues we a re talking about here. But frankly, you would not want to show the film of this meeting particularly , because it is a bit dry.
I do not know w hat you are trying to say, Jackie.
It has been quite interesting.

Q31 Y ou need to be able to distil things into three minutes , and t he beauty of PM Qs is that there are enough short clips to do that , which makes it easy news broadcasting to be truthful. I a m not doing myself any favours here am I really , now I am accusing them of being lazy.

Can I just add to that for the BBC, because we a re a big broadcaster, and we absolutely endeavour to get beyond just that noise. I f you think about “ Y esterday in Parliament ” and “ T oday in Parliament ”, for example, you wi ll get a very comprehensive, well - explained analytical piece about what happened in the H ouse, and I often listen to it the following day, and think, “Ah, I ha d n ’ t seen the whole context of that from the immediacy of the news coverage . ”
Q32 H ow many people hear that ?
I do n o t have the figures to hand.

But whenever people do , they always comment on it t o me, which is interesting . A gain , on u ser preferences , radio seems to be having a resurgence as a medium , and p erhaps we all need to think about how we do that b etter .
T o answer your point a little bit , it has a regular slot within the “ Today ” programme , which has very high audience figures across the week.
Ye s , but of course now everyone i s working from home they do not have to get up as early , s o they are not hearing it — just saying .
Thank you.
Q33 Is the Lobby itself a welcoming place for women?

Caroline Wheeler : Gosh, th at i s a big question . I found the whole experience of joining the Lobby so absolutely terrifying. I was very lucky because I came in from the regional press and so there were a lot of women in a similar position to me at the time. The reason for setting up the Women’s Lobby was that it can be a very daunting place for everybody, but in particular for women.

It definitely felt like a bit of a boys ’ club that I was coming into when I first joined , a nd I really appreciated having more women around me to help smooth that journey. Ce rtainly , one of the reasons why we wanted t he W omen ’ s Lobby there was to make sure that women did n o t feel intimidated coming into this world , so that they would see it as being very much an environment that was there just as much for them as it was for male reporters.

O ur ambition, as part of the W omen ’s Lobby , was to have a big network so that you can feel comfortable with us as well , w hich was another part of it, making sure that MPs , and particularly female MPs , did n o t feel intimidated about talking to journalists . W e wanted to provide a kind of welcome open arms to you guys t o o , to say , “ Come and talk to us , we are not going to bite — w ell, not always . ”

It is better than it was , and I a m really glad that we do have a Women’s Lobby there . I feel that we ha ve sign p osted it to female journalists now , and if they do need any support and help, they know there are senior female journalists there who will give them that kind of ear and shoulder to cry on. C ertainly , throughout my career I have had journalists come to me and just say, “ Can I have a cup of tea ?”, “C an I have a cup of coffee ?” if they want to talk about a particular issue . M aybe they a re not enjoying a certain aspect of their work , or they want advice on career progression — all of those things. W e have now created an environment where they do n o t feel as intimidated as perhaps some of us did many moons ago when we first arrived here.
Thank you . Kat y, d o you have anything to add to that?

J ust to say that within BBC Westminster I always encouraged a buddy system , s o if I had someone new coming into the unit, we woul d buddy up with Vick y, Laura or one of my more experienced female journalists to take them across to the H ouse and introduce to MPs.
I don’t really have anything to add .
Q34 You have answered quite a few of my questions already , with excellent responses. Do you think th at female journalists and editors treat stories about women in public life differently? Caroline.

It gets to the heart of what we said before : a story is a story . As I alluded to earlier, I a m aware that if I a m interviewing a male politician, I a m unlikely to start talking about what they a re wearing in the way that a male journalist will typically do — s tart talking about Liz’s clo thes, or whatever. I am perhaps more mindful of presenting what I a m reporting in a way that considers that kind of equality issue more thoroughly. In some senses these are the kind s of issues that maybe a male journalist simply would n o t think about. You almost become conditioned that when you go and do an interview with leading female politician, you ask them about what shoes or clothes they a re wearing, whereas a woman just instinctively would n o t do that.

I then instinctively tr y to make it my kind of schtick that if that was what male journalists were going to do, th en I was going to do the same to the m e n that I interviewed. But I do n o t think it i s necessarily something male journalists are conscious of in the way that I think women journalists would be when doing the same thing .

J ust to repeat what I said before, I was going to say that w e leave our gender at the door , which o f course is not true , b ut as much as we can a s journalists we approach stories as journalists, not as women or men.

I echo the point that a story is a story , but it is really important to have a mix of people making editorial decisions that reflects the audiences you a re serving, because men and women sometimes have a different take on things and a different interest i n things . Whether it is true that women are more interested in education , I do n o t know — plenty of men are as well. But quite often in editorial conferences I may raise things that perhaps my male colleagues would n o t have done , because I ha ve just got into work from dropping the kids off at school or whatever and they probably have n o t . I do not want to be stereotypical against men , as I a m sure there are plenty of men that take their c hildren to school . B ut it goes back to what I said before about making sure that we a re representing the people we a re broadcasting or writing for , a nd if you have a range of voices making the decisions about what is and is n o t a story, that to me is what we call a healthy press and a healthy society.

Q35 I have had conversations with or heard of stories where young women staffers have felt uncomfortable, or maybe ha d communications from older, more powerful men in this place , and I have done nothing about it. We can advise them where they should go, but for fear of recriminations , losing their job, being accused of being provocative , f or all those reasons, they choose not to take it any further. We know that Isabel Hardman, Cathy Newman and Charlotte Ev ans ha ve all spoken about similar things , and I have certainly heard about male colleagues and their attitude to women . Do female journalists feel comfortable about making complaints and actually go ing through a grievance procedure , or are they reluctant to do so because of the potential damage to their careers?

It i s hard to comment on that because I do n o t know what they a re thinking. I certainly have n ever spoken to a female journalist who has wanted to raise concerns but felt unable to do so. C ertainly , this H ouse has got better at recognising the issue in terms of sexual misconduct, and we now have the ICGS which ha s been created and is highlighted a lot. This is a broad er issue , which would not be exclusive to female journalists , nor i ndeed to female MPs. M ost people in this place find it very difficult to make complaints of that nature if they are at the junior end of things , largely because it can have an impact on their futures , which is something that the authorities are also aware of.

E ven for MPs there i s a disincentive to do it sometimes because it i s seen as creating ructions for a party , as rocking the boat and all of those things, but I do n o t think any of those issues are exclusive to the press , and in particular to female journalists. But I a m sure many of the attitudes that perm eate around this building , whether you are a staff member, an MP or an official, will be pretty similar.

There are obviously well reported examples in P arliament , and we all know that we ha ve been discussing them for some time now. From a journalistic perspective for the BBC, to answer your question directly I would say that n o journalist should fear for anything to do with their career if they have a potential cut - and - dried grievance . We have very strong HR procedures to follow along that, and that it should be a concern would quite simply not even come into my mind . A s a manager of people , I feel very strongly about that .

I do not have much to add to what t he others have said . No one sh ould be working in any place , in politics or anywhere else , where they feel in fear of bringing up some inappropriate behaviour because they a re worried about what that might do to their career . Not that they have, but i f anyone ever came to me and said , “ Look, this thing happened last night and I feel really uncomfortable about it , ” I would give them the support that I could and encourage them to seek re dress or to report it , and like the BBC we have pretty strong HR procedures in place to do that.

W e live in a society now where it is more likely that people will be open about stuff that happens to them th a n was perhaps the case in the past, and maybe slowly things change. But as I said, I would always support anybody who wanted to come forward but also understand why they would n o t .

Q36 M y understanding from conversations that I have had is that a lot of the women and young men who come forward now are coming forward with historical stories rather than contemporary stories . T here must be something which is quite empowering at the moment which is giving people the courage to come forward and say these things . A re you experiencing this with your colleagues : t hat when they were younger maybe staff let go because they thought it was not in their interest to say anything , but now, as they have matured and become more confident in their jobs , they are coming forward and saying things that happened to them when they were younger ?

Q37 I can no t comment on this one because actually a ll my colleagues are male , younger and newer to the profession than I am, so I have no experience of that. We do have a role to keep this in the spotlight , and The Sunday Times has probably done more than most of the newspapers in shining a light on the sexual misconduct that sadly does go on in this building. When there is momentum like that because there is media attention on it, then inevitably it does empower people to come forward , b ut I do n o t have any personal experience of that .

L ike wise, I have no personal experience , but I am sure that we would all agree it i s fair to say that attitudes across society ha ve changed quite significantly in the last 10 or 20 years, which no doubt enables people to come forward.

We tend to put up with less and do not just accept things as we get older — that is the glory that comes with age and confidence. But again, things have changed , and I would maybe encourage other people to come forward.

Q38 I am conscious that we are going to lose Caroline at 4 pm , s o I am going to direct this to you very quickly. Things have changed , but have things changed enough in the Lobby itself? You refer red to providing a shoulder to cry on , and Katy referred to a buddy system. How would you feel if younger women were complaining about sexual harassment and misconduct within the Lobby itself from older , more experience d and p erhaps more powerful members of the Lobby ?

A bsolutely appalled . It is not something that I have come across , but there have been numerous but very rare incidences where there have been issues of the nature that you ha ve described raised in the Lobby . I can no t think of that happening in the last five or six years , c ertainly . A gain, speaking to your point about having a pass and adhering to what is expected of you and your behaviour on the Estate , people are generally mindful that conduct must be in keeping with what the Commons authorities require.

In answer to the question about whether things have got better , yes they are better , largely because there are more women here and our voice has got louder. T he W omen ’ s Lobby has enabled that to happen t o a certain extent . I t i s still not perfect ; w e a re still outnumbered. I once made a very bad joke which went down like a lead balloon at one particular meeting , where I said that in the Sunday Lobby there were still more men with one eye than there were wo men — I did have the permission of the gentleman concerned to say this. B ut we ar e still not there , and it always ebbs and flows in terms of women coming in and out , because people leave to have c hildren , go on maternity leave and do n o t come back.

Q39 Do you ever worry about the rapidity with which some young women move around o rganisations within the Lobby ? D o you assume that it i s just for their career purposes, o r perhaps they are deliberately moving to get away from older senior male members ?

I genuinely have never had another female journalist come to me and raise the concern that you a re suggesting . W omen do move around , a nd part of that is because we are still a minority. T here is now a greater recognition on editorial Lobby teams in particular that they do need to have some female representation . A s I say, it is better , b ut for many years there have been all male teams on some of the biggest national newspapers. Thankfully that i s no longer the case, and there is better representation.

We are still not anywhere near parity, which i s obviously what we need to be aiming towards. But generally there is appreciation of the fact that it i s a good thing to have a woman on your team . I should add that it is not that they are being employed simply because they are women, but there is a n understanding that it is a good thing to have a senior female member on your team, which is to be applauded and welcomed.
Q40 Thank you, and we will let you go at 4 pm. S orry, I a m going to keep Kat y and Cristina. Kat y , did you have anything to add about the buddy system ?

Thank you, Chair . I would just like to clarify what I meant by the buddy system , because it was n o t actually in relation to harassment but very much in relation to learning the job , and going back to Caroline ’ s point about how she found it intimidating . T o clear that up, I a m not talking about intimidation , but really just about how do you help someone who is new to Westminster ?
It is about how to n avigate the culture and understand how it works.
Exactly , a nd it i s true for women and women , women and men , and men and men as well.

Q41 I want to ask some questions about your regulators. How does Ofcom’s code h elp you to decide whether or not and how to report stories that are potentially sexist or misogynistic in content , and perhaps your own codes and standards as well ? Cristina .

The Ofcom code is very detailed, and I do not have it all in front of me. I can always follow up with paragraphs that I can send to you. But we are basically not allowed to report anything that i s discriminatory , a nd therefore Ofcom is quite a standard. I have found it . Section 3 says: “ In applying generally accepted standards, broadcasters must ensure material which may cause offence is justified by its context … S uch material may include, but is not limited to , offensive language, violence, sexual violence , violation of human rights ” et cetera, so t he code is quite clear, and there is a fairly established complaints procedure that people can complain to Ofcom. There i s a n Ofcom c ommittee that will then decide whether there are grounds for that complaint. It i s then thoroughly investigated , t hey can take all sorts of documents away from you, can have access to emails and so on. It provides us with a very clear code by which to write our editorial content .

Q42 T o your knowledge —this is to each of you— has Ofcom ever sanctioned anyone for sexist or otherwise discriminatory reporting , or for perpetuating negative stereotypes in any of their programmes?
Not at Sky Ne ws in recent years.
Not in my memory .
Q43 A nyone else that you might have reported on ?

N ot in my memory. Could I just add one more thing ? It is to echo Cristina, but also to say the relationship is in a partnership . We begin really with the partnership of the editorial standards and guidelines for the BBC, which obviously has strict guidelines around this area. As Cristina says, overall we a re regulated by Ofcom as part of that partnership.
Thank you . That is all from me, Chair.

T hank you. I think we had a follow - up question for Caroline about how T he T imes is regulat ed, but as she has had to leave us , w e will leave it there. Can I take this opportunity to thank you for your answers , which ha ve been really informative ? If t here i s anything you want to add in writing afterwards , d o please feel free . I will now draw the meeting to a close .
