I have one anecdote: two years ago I was in Eswatini and , 2 3 years after the divorce between the FCO and DfID , people still told me about the first meeting of the h igh c ommissioner and the head of the DfID office with the K ing, when these two people had a stand - up row about who would be H is M ajesty ’ s principal interlocutor now that they were two departments. That is just basically wrong.
It does not take a massive reorganisation to solve such problems.

Q18 We talked a lot about the difficulties of merger when there are budgetary constraints and even cuts, as you said. I want to ask about two other issues, one of which Lord Stirrup raised. First, it is just not true that we speak with one voice internationally, even after the merger. After all, some of the most major ambitions the Government have internationally are n othing to do with either the Foreign Office or the former DfID, now all the FCDO— climate change , for example . On Ukraine, the Home Office has a trump hand with its migration policy. On trade, after Brexit the G overnment ’ s main ambition was to strike trade deals all over the world, which was outside the FCDO structure. We have a huge “speaking with one voice” problem, irrespective of the FCDO merger.

Secondly, Ukraine marks the return of hard security to our conception of foreign policy i n terms of public profile and priority ; it never disappeared for wise Foreign Office people. If you were a former DfID official now working in the merged FCDO , might you not think that the ambition for cultural merger , at a time when security is coming to dominate foreign policy and a time of scarce resource s— put all those things together — seems quite a threat to the mission of what you do day in , day out as part of what used to be called DfID and is now development activity within FCDO ?

I have a couple of points. First, yes, speaking with multiple voices is a problem, but w e should be consciously striving to have one voice. It can be difficult, but our impact is greater when we have had internal debates and the external messaging is joined up.

On your culture point, looking at what is happening in Ukraine is clearly the first chapter. As Bronwen said , when we look ahead , the task of reconstruction is something that DfID is familiar with. If you look at that crisis over a few years, all parts of the new department will see their relevance.

For q uite a few years, including during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, there was an element of British development policy that looked towards those regions and what Britain could do in helping them redevelop, so i t is not completely new to ask whether development policy is going to be bent in that direction. You have caught something about the urgency — we touched on it before —and whether the immediate takes precedence over things that have a longer - term horizon. That is inevitable but I think people are very conscious of that, and it is to be resisted.

On the question of speaking with one voice, overall that is probably not going to happen because there are many parts of B ritain ’ s voice abroad, as you said, but it means that in some countries you can have a more joined - up conversation, even if, for example, it is a case of: d o we want to talk to the Taliban? No. Do we still want to give aid to Afghanistan? Perhaps, yes. At least it will happen in a more joined - up way, not in two completely separate wings of the G overnment. The value seems to be o n those things .

Q19 My question follows that directly. My concern is that this is an old solution, a retro solution, to an old problem. David Cameron, who I worked with in No. 10, introduced the N ational Security Council to try to solve this exact problem of security-related departments all doing their own thing. To some extent, my concern is that the re-merger of DfID has made it worse, not better. Not only are we having problems with its identity and what it is able to do, but I am not clear that some of those wide ambitions on climate, health, conflict r esolution , conflict prevention and pandemic prevention are better placed within the Foreign Office than under the auspices of the National Security Council . To what extent is the National Security Council working with a distinct voice?

My experience of the National Security Council is that its effectiveness depends entirely on the chairman. Looking at the agenda of the National Security Council, it has a job to do in deciding what is for it — those subjects that need cross - Whitehall co - ordination — and what is for departments. I agree strongly that some issues would be better left to departments, and then the NSC could concentrate on two or three priorities rather than trying to spread itself thinly across the whole policy front.

I do not think that there is a structure that preserves or annihilates a development strategy. The question is what that development strategy is. What are our priorities going to be in a world that has changed quite a lot in the past couple of years , with many claims on whatever development money we have, whether 0 .5% or 0 .7%? Structure matters, but it does not determine the policy and it does not even determine the primacy of the policy. What determines that is the Government saying, “This is what we are going to do in development. We care about this and it is going to go ahead”. The many possible answers to that at the moment, a nd the fact that the world is changing , are among the things that have left British development a bit confused and left those people within the FCDO vulnerable. Their mission is less clear at the moment. As we ha ve just been talking about, suddenly this great urgency of Ukraine has arisen. What is needed to make the merger work better is not a different structure but a clear statement of priorities on development.

Q20 Lord McDonald, during your five years as head of the FCO, how many ambassadors or high commissioners from DfID did you appoint? And then a silly question: would you expect, after the merger, mainstream FCO people to dominate all the senior ambassador positions?

I do not have a precise figure but there were some striking high - profile examples : the high commissioner in Nigeria, the ambassador in Zimbabwe, the high commissioner in Tanzania, the ambassador in Indonesia , the G overnor of St Helena and the ambassador in Ethiopia were all DfID people . So there was a sprinkling across the world, mostly in Africa and mostly in countries where development looms large in our relationship. The one appointment in the other direction was Matthew Rycroft as Permanent Secretary.

Would you expect , under the merger — if we can talk of mainstream FCO people in future —more senior positions to be able to be filled, such as high commissioners or ambassadors , by people with an aid and development interest?
My point is that that is already happening and I believe it has increased since the merger, particularly in Africa , although i deally it should not be on just one continent.

Q21 I would like to raise the question of whether these new structures have the necessary amount of flexibility. I have in mind the question of l andmines , which you mentioned. The remarkable thing is that Halo — I declare my interest as an ambassador for it—extraordinarily has a deal with the Taliban to continue its efforts in Afghanistan, yet the finance for that comes from both Germany and the US.

The other issue, which was raised by Lord Boaten g, is that Barbados, which is going to be a republic , is in receipt of money from China . I understand that Jamaica, which has said rather bluntly to the Duke of Cambridge, “We ’ re going to be an independent country, we ’ re going to be a republic” , is also in line to get some support from China. O thers use financial support as a way of creating political influence . That is not our sole objective but there are occasions where you get two for the price of one—that is, you achieve the development objectives but also maintain influence. Are you satisfied that the new arrangements are flexible enough to recognise these opportunities?

That is the intention. You mentioned the Caribbean. I have another anecdote. We have just re opened in Antigua and Barbuda, and I was one of the first people through. The most interesting thing that I discovered is that every year China gives 15 full scholarships to the brightest sixth- formers in A ntigua . That means that in 20 years that country will be run by people trained in Beijing. For 20 years we were completely absent. We need to be on the ground. I think the new department is more on the ground in more places, and that will help.

That anecdote is an example of how it can work well for Britain, but what you have touched on is the old furious row at the heart of how development aid is deployed. The reason why DfID was set up separately —this is the culture that it then developed very strongly — was to say, “We don ’ t want this contaminated by questions of national interest. We want to deal with poverty reduction. We ’ re going to follow that brief irrespective of questions of the interest of the UK”.

You are asking whether there can be times where there are, as you put it, two for one. Undoubtedly there can, and that anecdote is a good example . The question is whether you lose something at the same time by pursuing that. Again, we come back to what the national intent is for our development aid. You can lose the pursuit of poverty reduction by considering only how to get leverage on other Governments.

Surely a sophisticated organisation such as the one we have just created is capable of identifying both objectives. It is the old saying: i f you cannot ride two horses at once, you should not be in the bloody circus. Surely we ought to be capable of that . Do you think this organisation will be?
I think it will be.

I would not rush to accuse the Foreign Office of a lack of sophistication or worldliness. I am sure it can see those dilemmas. I think this is a political decision about what we are doing with this development aid . I am sure it can spot those opportunities. This is really about the purpose of Britain ’ s development aid, and there is not a structure that is going to answer that. I can give you my own views about what I think development aid should be for, but that is not really what we are discussing today . For me, t here is no structure that substitutes the central question of what we are trying to do with Britain ’ s development aid.
I hope you do not mind if we trespass on your time for a few minutes longer so that we can have the last question from Baroness Blackstone.

Q22 The previous witnesses today said firmly and strongly that one of the problems that they, representing the development world and aid agencies, were experiencing was a lack of transparency from the new merged department, and that there was a big difference in this respect between DfID and the Foreign Office. If you are going to get a synthesis of cultures, which Lord McDonald mentioned, i s there a need to try to become closer on the issue of transparency? Maybe you do not agree that there is a difference, but if there is then perhaps it is something that should be addressed.
The Foreign Office needed to be more transparent and the new department needs to be transparent . I agree strongly with that.

I also agree strongly. At the point when this merger was done, there was far too little communication about the effects of the cut in development aid. That was launched very suddenly , without a lot of discussion , on government departments but also on NGOs and so on by the Foreign Secretar y at the time, Dominic Raab , and his team.
Presumably a restoration of the cuts to the development budget will help . Some of the confusion for the aid agencies is caused by sudden huge reductions or being cut out altogether.

That is an interesting point but it is not so easily turned back on. These are projects that have been interrupted . Contracts have been ended on the ground and employment ended . You cannot just switch it back on; these projects took years to build up.

That is true . Sometimes the problem is not transparency ; it is that in the department they really do not know what the key principles are going to be and what the final decisions are. Instead of sharing that, they look inscrutable, so people feel deceived or let down . Sometimes it is ignoran ce, not a lack of transparency.
Bronwen Maddo x : I do not find that very reassuring .
I am feeling liberated in my retirement.

It is my privilege to thank both our witnesses for this second session. Perhaps I might just be permitted a personal comment w ith regard to how it is seen from this side of the Room by someone who has been in both opposition and government. Lord McDonald, in the two years that I was a Minister at the Foreign Office I always considered that there was a lot of clarity about decision-making from the top and who to go to if I was unhappy about anything — which was very rare — and I was confident that it would be resolved, which it always was. When I went to DExEU, where there was a Second Permanent Secretary, that clarity disappeared fast, so I can see the difference.

The first time that I came across the work of the Institute for Government first - hand was in the latter days of the Gordon Brown Administration. I learned there the way in which the Institute for Government operates open - handed ly and even - handed ly with all politicians to provide guidance about good governance. I am very much aware that it is then down to those of us who are politicians either to take that advice or perhaps to make the mistake of not doing so. Thank you very much indeed.

sessions.iT: Impact of merging of the Foreign & Commonwealth Office and the Department for International Development
sessions.w: Stephanie Draper (Bond); Simon Starling (Bond)

segs.tx: International Relations and Defence Committee
Corrected oral evidence: Impact of merging of the Foreign & Commonwealth Office and the Department for International Development
Wednesday 30 March 2022
Watch the meeting: https://parliamentlive.tv/event/index/1a054ba9-40e3-4d6a-9b8f-a558edc5e069

Members present: Baroness Anelay of St Johns ( The Chair) ; Lord Alton of Liverpool ; Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Blackstone ; Lord Boateng; Lord Campbell of Pittenweem ; Baroness Fall ; Baroness Rawlings ; Lord Stirrup; Baroness S ugg; Lord Teverson ; Lord Wood of Anfield .
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 - 10
Witnesses
I : Stephanie Draper, Chief Executive, Bond; Simon Starling, Director of Policy and Advocacy, Bond .
Examination of witnesses
Stephanie Draper and Simon Starling .

Q1 Good morning. I welcome to this meeting of the International Relations and Defence Select Committee in the House of Lords Stephanie Draper, c hief executive at B ond, the UK network for approximately 400 organisations large and small that are working in i nternational d evelopment, and Simon Starling, director of policy and advocacy a t B ond. Thank you for joining us today to give evidence for our session examining the impact of the merger of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office with the D epartment for International Development. It is an appropriate time to take a look at this matter because the FCDO , as it is now, is facing its greatest diplomatic challenges for decades a s we see President Putin launch an illegal war against Ukraine, showering civilians and hospitals with indiscriminate bombing using missiles.

Our witnesses and committee members will of course have to ensure that we remember that this session is on the record, transcribed and broadcast as usual. I also remind members to declare any relevant interest s before asking their questions today.

I will begin , as ever , by asking a question that is rather broad in scope , then turn to my colleagues for more detailed questions. I anticipate that throughout this session, which will l ast until 11 am, when my colleagues ask a question they may wish to ask a linked supplementary question.

The general question is: d oes the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office appear to have a different approach to the goals and delivery of overseas aid from the approach that DfID took ? Are there examples of where foreign and security policy appear s to have taken precedence over development priorities since the merger took place? Stephanie , may I start with you? I appreciate that your time is limited until 11 am , and then your colleague Simon will stay with us until 11.30 am.

Thank you, and a pologies that I could not be there with you in person. Does the FCDO appear to have a different approach to development from Df ID? It does. The merger was explicitly intended to change our approach to overseas aid, aligning diplomacy with broader international activities and bringing those things together, as per the integrated review. Although we were not supportive of the merger at the time, it is an opportunity because achieving a sustainable future and a just and fair world requires all the international toolkit. But we have seen that development priorities seem to take a back seat when it comes to a number of immediate, more urgent , pressing priorities. You mentioned Ukraine a s a good example of that.

We still do not have from the new department an i nternational d evelopment strategy. That suggests to me that it is not at the heart of the new department. We are told that it is coming , but it has been a long time in fruition following the integrated review published in March 2021. That is a big gap for us.

We have also seen development priorities shrinking. We had seven priorities initially when the department was merged . The current F oreign S ecretary states three current priorities: women and girls, humanitarian , and green infrastructure. That narrow s the focus o f i nternational d evelopment, which is a core part of the system that the integrated review reflects. That is concerning to us, and we are waiting to see how the fuller i nternational d evelopment strategy works.

In the integrated review we also did not see a very strong focus on development . We think that is a real missed opportunity , because d evelopment is really underutilised in conne ct ion with defence and diplomacy. It is about building the foundations of a safer and fairer world, and a lot of that is really cost effective. Prevention, be that conflict prevention or supporting states before they are in crisis , pre-fragility, is underserved in not bringing development further to the fore . There are lots of existing strategies within Df ID, such as a commitment to 50% of our overseas development assistance going to fragile states and commitments to the SDGs and “leave no one behind ”, which are much less to the fo re . That 50% commitment has not been carried forward into the FC DO .

One exception that we are pleased to see is the FC DO disability inclusion and rights strategy, which was brought on board in February. That is great and has been welcomed by those working on disability rights. We have not seen how that translates into practi c e, but it is a good sign.

Overall , it is less to the fore. That focus on those central organising principles that give you a systemic view, such as the sustainable d evelopment g oals and a poverty focus , has declined in the new department.
Thank you. Mr Starling, do you wish to add anything to that?

Yes. I will add just a couple of things. As Stephanie says and as you all know, international development is a long-term, complex challenge. Changing priorities on a regular basis is not that helpful, so we are waiting to see the international development strategy. We will review that and make a judgment on how things are looking then. In practi c e, what has happened is that quite a lot of very big decisions have been made before the strategy has come out, so the strategy is not driving the decisions . Rather, political choices are driving the decisions being made.

As you know, th e merger was largely overshadowed by the cuts to the aid budget ; about a third of the aid budget has gone. The NAO report that comes out tomorrow on the management of the aid cuts process will be interesting reading . The cut to the bilateral aid programme is huge; i t is about half. That is the context in which we are waiting to see the new strategy. Obviously , decisions are having to be made in advance of that, and the decisions that we are seeing are largely a change from what we saw under Df ID. Under Df ID there was a very strong focus on the sustainable development goals and on leaving no one behind, reaching the furthest behind first . That poverty focus was really baked into Df ID and was well respected across the world. Stephanie mentioned the 50% focus on fragile and conflict-affected states.

The realities are that we are cutting our aid programme to many of the world ’ s poorest countries. About 36 African countries get no UK a i d since the aid cuts last year, and that includes many of the poorest countries in the world —in the Sahel, for example . We have hugely pulled out of countries in the Middle East. We definitely worry that there is less focus on where the need is greatest and more focus on where it is in the UK ’ s national and security interest s . The balance between where the money goes is now focused less on the poorest countries and more on middle-income countries. For us that is a concern because, in the long term , ignoring the poorest, most fragile and most conflict-affected countries w ill come back to bite us. There will be humanitarian emergencies and we will have to try to respond to those crises in the long term. Prevention is always cheaper than cure. We think that a focus away from some of those structural , long - term development issues is a bit short - sighted . We are looking forward to seeing how that will be addressed in the i nternational d evelopment strategy.

Thank you very much for putting your answers in the context of the expected strategy on aid. We have already noted that the language has changed. A couple of weeks ago the Government were talking in terms of the strategy be ing published “ very shortly ”; in the letter from the F oreign S ecretary to us just last week , that has now slipped back to “in the spring” . Clearly we have a long time to wait for it yet.

Q2 In a sense you have partially answered my question, but I wonder whether I can push you to take what you said a little further. First, can you comment on the Government ’ s apparent objective for a cultural merger between the two departments? As far as you can see, has the culture of DfID had any kind of impact on the way in which the merged department operates—its vision and values, and so on? I wonder whether you can put a little more fl e sh on what you were implying earlier, which was that development really is not at the heart of the new department and has to some extent be en sidelined . If you could illustrate that, it would be helpful to the committee.

W e saw that th e culture merger was moving ahead and was then thrown off by the aid cuts. That really undermined the bringing together of the new department , because it was such a massive process . Lots of things have diverted from bringing those two cultures together to the benefit of the UK and the world.

There are a few examples. One of the things that we think was really leading within Df ID was transparency and being accountable to the British people and the people we work with for the aid budget. DfID consistently received a very good rating in the Aid Transparency Index , while the Foreign Office, as was, received a fair rating. That is one of the indicators that we have been looking at to review how well the merger has gone.

We have 15 hallmarks that we have been tracking, and a lot of them are depend e nt on the i nternational d evelopment strategy . On our last assessment, which was six months in, we said that two were met, eight were partially met and five were not met. One of the ones we are concerned about is transparency. W e have not seen transparency on how the ODA budget is being spent. We are hearing reports of things such as NGOs not being able to speak about their work, and the data on the cuts has been very fragmented and inconsistent. The new department is not as transparent and accountable as Df ID was.

We have also seen that engagement with civil society is somewhat patchy. That has improved under the current F oreign S ecretary. It was pretty woeful once the new department was merged, but now we are seeing more of that engagement, which we think is a really important cultural piece. We have been able to add value in dialogue on Afghanistan, for example, bringing in on -the- ground experience, being able to bring together a number of agendas and engaging on things such as the Summit for D emocracy.

The final cultural element is the make - up of the leadership team . After six months , two out of eight director s- general had development backgrounds. We now have Moazzam Malik l eaving the leadership team but N ick Dyer j oining, so that maintains some development expertise. The other element of that culture is: do we have the expertise, the staff and the resourcing staying within the department and being able to add value? That starts with the leadership team , and w e are still concerned about the balance of that . We understand from reports that a number of Df ID staff have left, so there has been something of a brain drain as well, which does not give that real strength of merging two cultures , rather than one culture taking over the other.

I am interested in your final point about what you called a brain drain of DfID staff. Are these senior people who had a leadership role in the former department, or mainly younger people? Why are they going?

I do not know the answer to that question. Devex reported in September that 213 DfID staff had left since the merger, and w e see that leaving continue. They are in specialist areas such as nutrition, WASH , and sexual and reproductive health. It is that real expertise that seems to be leaving the department, which has been a model of UK leadership around the world.
And they are not being replaced by other people with similar expertise, as far as you know.

One of the things we are seeing, in practical terms, is that there are a lot of vacancies; the merger is not fully operational. You might be losing that long-term expertise, which is more difficult to replace, but it is also happening in areas such as procurement. We understand that nearly a fifth of the procurement department jobs are vacant. A lot of things still need to be worked out. That makes things more difficult and makes our focus on development more difficult to maintain.

I apologise for the noises off. We have a generator outside, and clearly the dustbin men and women have just arrived. Apologies for any interruption to the sound quality. It is not the fault of the technicians sitting behind me; it is outside.

Q3 Thank you for joining us. You talked about the recent improved engagement with civil society under the new Foreign Secretary. Can you say a bit more about the impact of the merger on delivery partners hips with aid agencies? How has the fact that aid agencies are now working with what is the main organ of the UK ’ s diplomatic service affected those relationships?

It is mixed. In reality, we are seeing that , from a delivery partner perspective , there is a lot of uncertainty. Df ID and FCO teams are still operating separately. Although everything is branded FCDO , there are still different templates , policies and approaches . That is more complicated to deal with, as it is not always clear where to submit information or find out about opportunities. At the same time, that loss of institutional knowledge means that we spend time having to explain to former FCO staff how our work works, what the development challenges are and how work needs to be more long term . There are lots of those sorts of anecdotal examples; our members are having to spend more time working through and explaining work as delivery partners than they had to before . That is how that is working practically on the ground.

Then we have things such as the business planning process taking longer because we did not have the ID S, so there is greater uncertainty . Budget projects are still being allocated at the moment , so no decisions have been made. For really impactful long - term projects, you need that certainty to keep moving; y ou cannot be pausing every so often. We had a period of annual budgeting , which we hope will be improved now that we are into slightly longer budget cycles. I do not know whether Simon wants to add anything to that.

There are still some different systems in operation, which makes it m ore challenging for delivery partners to engage. During the period of the aid cuts, communication from the FCDO was very limited , so c ommunication and trust need to be rebuilt a little . Normal service has not yet resumed, so there has been a very disruptive period. The FCDO is still trying to merge the systems together and there have been lots of changes in staff , so relationships with delivery partners have changed. Delivery partners have been in the dark about whether their programmes will continue i n the longer term. As Stephanie said, the general relationships between civil society and the FCDO are starting to improve now, but there are still some gaps as the merger becomes more operational.

To follow up on that point, there have been various rounds of cuts. The first were with the reduction in GNI because of the pandemic, and then there was the cut from 0.7% to 0.5%. That first one was done when there was a DfID and the second when there was an FCDO. Can you reflect on the difference you have felt, on the decisions around the cuts, since the merger?

When it was DfID there was more engagement with civil society around the cuts, but it was still hard to understand exactly what was happening during those cuts. In t he last round of cuts, we have had very little information and transparency has been very low. It is still not clear where the money is being spent. We are still having to piece together to get a complete picture of where the cuts have happened , where various pieces of funding are continuing and where those allocations are happening.
T he Chair: Thank you. Simon, do you have anything to add to that?

I support what Stephanie said. The cut from 0.7% to 0.5% was such a huge cut—around £4 billion—in quite a short timeframe. Obviously, we would have preferred more engagement about how those choices were being made. It left organisations not knowing; the uncertainty was a problem. People had to close programmes because they did not know what was going to happen. That lack of transparency and the speed of that process were challenging for us all, and I think that is what the NAO report tomorrow will focus on. It will be interesting to look at that.

Q4 We have talked a bit about the relationship with delivery partners. I am interested in what you think about the lack of a specific Minister on the world stage and how that is affecting our reputation. You mentioned accountability. Within Parliament and at home, having a joint Minister leads to just one round of questions, not two. I am interested in your thoughts on that.

We think that we really suffer from not having a Cabinet-level Minister for international development. To come back to the cuts, the cuts to the ODA budget mean that we are less able to respond to increasing numbers of humanitarian crises around the world , whether driven by conflict or climate . That is very much coming to the fore with needing to find , rightly, additional funds for Ukraine on top of Afghanistan , the existing crises in Yemen and the coming famine —i t is not coming any more — in the Horn of Africa. If that had been brought to the fore in the C abinet, a different decision might have been made.

With the best will in the world, the Foreign Secretary has many responsibilities . S he is also Secretary of State for E qualit ies and Brexit, and she has been focused on visiting countries that are about our relationship on security, technology or trade. Liz Truss has visited India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Australia, Russia, Estonia and the US . That is an appropriate focus for a F oreign S ecretary, but a M inister for Development would visit very different places and bring a different long - term perspective to the C abinet. We think that is something that could easily be addressed and would add real value to the UK and to the people we work with.

This comes to the core of what, for me, is an uneasy decision. It was interesting that Tony Blair, who first set up D fID, said in his memoir, I think correctly, that he had sort of created his own NGO, and there were issues with that. But the problem with it going back to the FCDO is that , although having aligned foreign policies is absolutely what we want, i f you want to prevent humanitarian cris e s — conflict, famine , climate chan ge— that does not necessarily mean working with some of your top trade partners , or even your top partners on the diplomatic side. T o what extent is this a problem that is less about moving department than about how they actually solve those issues within them?

The structure does not necessarily dictate the decisions that are made. What has happened is that there has been a loss of a long - term perspective. We all know that as leaders you have to balance what is right in front of you with what is going to benefit the world and address local challenges , such as climate change and inequality , in the longer term. Gordon Brown said there was a risk of the UK losing long - term soft power with a focus on short - term foreign policy goals, and there have been so many short - term foreign policy goals that it is very difficult for the senior level of that department to maintain a focus on the long - term benefits.

There are advantages to the merger that could be capitalised on. On Afghanistan, we had joint meetings that meant we were able to get political briefings and understand what was happening while they were able to understand what was happening on the ground , but it still took a long time. More specifically, you would think that bringing humanitarian work and sanctions together would work really well and we would get immediate exceptions for humanitarian s as part of the sanctions regime, but that still took months to happen ; indeed , it happened only after a UN resolution. Those benefits happen at the strategic level but also at the operational level. There is an opportunity for the IDS to address that , but if we had senior Cabinet responsibility then that could balance that out too.
I appreciate that Stephanie has to leave us, and I thank her. Simon, is there anything you would like to add?

T he job titles of the Ministers within the FCDO are slightly terrifying. Steph mentioned Liz Truss ’ s range of responsibilities . James Cleverly has responsibility for international development but he also has defence, international security, trade , Europe, North America , Russia and Iran. Any one of those—for instance, Russia or Iran—could easily take precedence in the short term, and it is then very difficult for the senior leadership team to maintain a f ocus on the sort of long - term structural issues that ultimately we would all benefit from addressing. That is one of the challenges of the merger : how do you retain the long - term structural inequality and poverty - alleviation focus while there are so many urgent foreign policy issues and crises taking up senior leadership attention?

Q5 In response to Baroness Fall ’ s point, which I do not necessarily expect Simon to comment on, I do not think DfID ever saw itself as Tony Blair ’ s NGO. T hat is for another day, when perhaps Lord Wood would comment on that too.

I should declare an interest as chancellor of the University of Greenwich, which houses the Natural Resources Institute, and as chair of Water & Sanitation for the Urban Poor, both of which are and have been in receipt of DfID defunding and now FCDO funding.

I wonder if you could help us on this question : w hat have been the budgetary consequences of the merger? In practi c e , has it facilitated the transfer of funds from former DfID programmes to non-DfID activities ? You described the responsibilities of Ministers, so there might be occasions when that transfer has occur r ed. Are the budgets still ring - fenced?

That is a great question and I am not sure we will be in a position to give much of an answer to it, partly because of the lack of transparency about how the money is being spent. There is also a time lag in the official ODA statistics coming out , so we will not really see the detail for some time . We do not know.

What we can say is that transparency has been low and that the overall picture , as we talked about before , is that the big reduction to the ODA budget , and to bilateral programmes in particular , has meant that in practice some areas have been ring - fenced and protected. Those areas are largely the priorities of the Foreign Secretary , while the areas that appear to be taking the biggest cuts are the bilateral aid programmes. Although it is difficult to comment on specifics , such as movements between the FCDO and former DfID programmes , the development programmes are definitely taking a big hit in comparison to some of the areas that are priorities . For example, the Foreign Secretary is very keen on investment and B II , so that has had a budget increase, while at the same time we are seeing UK aid withdrawn from 36 countries in Africa and several 12 across the Middle East . So we are seeing quite a lot of practical ramifications of that aid cut, and ch oices are being made in that ahead of the aid strategy.

In terms of the transfer of funds, does Bond h ave any sympathy for the point made by many Caribbean and small - island Heads of Government , who are confronting real issues around sustainable development, that they have not qualified in the past for DfID defunding because of the definition of ODA , yet by any stretch of the imagination — certainly all the evidence of one ’ s eyes would demonstrate this—they are actually far from rich countries and are confronted by issues in relation to climate change and environmental sustainability that have not in the past been met by DfID ? Has the FCDO shown any indication of a willingness to vire funds in favour of such small island state s?

That is a good question and I do not know the answer. The general trend is towards a focus on future trading partners, so we are seeing less money go into the poorest countries and those that do not have a much of a strategic or trading interest with the UK , and more investment in some of the countries where the UK has other interests, such as trade. Small island state s may not feature much in the trade picture. The areas that we know the Foreign Secretary is interested in are around investment and security, and those are the countries that seem to be continuing to—
Have the environment and climate change not featured? T he Government as a whole are supposed to be interested in that.

They are, and it will be interesting to see how that pans out in the international development strategy. We have been pushing very hard to make sure that c limate change is not dropped from that strategy. It is a government priority so you would expect it not to be but we are now talking about a very squeezed budget, with difficult choices about where the money is going to come from. Where is the money go ing to come from to pay for the huge crisis in Ukraine — out of the climate change budget or the African bilateral programme? Some r eally difficult choices are going to have to be made.

Q6 Mr Starling, can I tempt you to say something about the recently announced changes to the FCDO ’ s structure, which seem, to the observer anyway, to be yet another disruptive round of musical chairs? What does that say about the success of the merger? In your view, will that restructure solve any of the challenges and problems that have arisen as a result of the merger?

Stephanie covered some of this before. A more senior - level focus on development is good . The fact that only two of the eight in the leadership team have development experience is a worry for us. We want to see that C abinet - level responsibility so that development is not lost from the FCDO . Although we would not say too much on the movement of the chairs at senior level, the concern for us would be that it is a signal of the direction of travel : t he foreign policy concerns are going to take precedence over the development concerns, and we will lose that longer - term expertise.

We also worry about the partly understandable shift to focus on geopolitics and security as a result of the Russian invasion of Ukraine . There is a challenge in responding to that in the FCDO while not losing the previous focus on helping those most in need around the world. That will be a n ongoing challenge for the FCDO, for sure.

The other thing is that we hope the restructure does not impact on other areas. There are rumours that some really important directorates and departments might be under threat. We do not want to see wider , big changes to the FCDO portfolio . F or example, there is talk about the office for conflict stabilisation and mediation, w hich we think is super important. I do not want to comment too much on changes of position at the top, but we must make sure that we do not lose that commitment to and expertise on long - term development or lose expertise in further key areas in the FCDO.

One of the arguments for the merger that was put at the time was that it would consolidate the political ability to resolve conflict, for instance in places such as Tigray. It is not a natural catastrophe but a manmade disaster; starvation is being used as a weapon of war and being are dying in large numbers. Have you seen any evidence whatever that the amalgamation of DfID with the FCO has made any tangible difference in situations such as that, or in northern Nigeria? You also mentioned the Sahel.

It might be too early to tell. There are definitely advantages to that join t approach. We have been working closely with the FCDO around the Afghanistan crisis. The FCDO was quick to set up a task force that covered all the key areas of the response, and that included the foreign policy approach as well. That was really useful ; we were not dealing with two different departments in a crisis, so that was helpful.

The challenge around that was that the ways of working are still not quite embedded. For example, w e saw that within the sanctions and humanitarian access piece that Stephanie mentioned earlier. There are big concerns about ensuring that aid money does not go to the Taliban . Those c oncerns and the sanctions effectively led to aid agencies being unable to operate quickly enough. That hindered the response and slowed it down. There are definitely lessons to be learned on that but there is definitely potential, although it is perhaps a little early to tell .

Ministers also told us that empowering our ambassadors on the ground in places such as Pakistan, for instance, which has a huge aid budget, would enable those ambassadors to look as though they had some control over funding and to have greater political edge in the way they were able to take decisions. Is that your experience?
Again, it is probably too early to say on that. I do not want to comment too much on the in - country picture without a bit more knowledge of what has been happening.

Before I turn to Lord Stirrup for the last in our formal run of questions, I will say that if we have time I will open it up for questions more broadly and give precedence to colleagues who have not yet had the opportunity to ask a question. I see that Lord Campbell has already indicated that he has a question.

Q7 W e have touched once or twice this morning on the crisis in Ukraine. From a number of the previous answers , I have the sense that it is perhaps too early in the process of this reorganisation to tell exactly how successful it is going to be. On a number of occasions you have pointed to the fact that a number of posts are not even filled in the department. I t is still an emerging picture , but one would have thought that the crisis in Ukraine would be an excellent example of how a combined Foreign Office and Df ID can work effectively together . It is one of the greatest foreign policy challenges the UK has faced in recent years but also a huge humanitarian crisis . The crisis is not confined just to Ukraine , of course; with the number of migrants flooding into Poland and other countries, it is spreading further. Have you seen any evidence of such a joined - up approach emerging from the combined FCDO ? If not , what further action would you like to see?

One of the positives was that the FCDO reached out early on to B ond to start co - ordinating with civil society , which operates a lot of the programmes on the ground in and around Ukraine. We set up co - ordination mechanisms pretty quickly to have those conversations about how the humanitarian response can be delivered. That was a positive sign.

It is a little early to say how the FCDO has responded to the Ukraine crisis as a whole . It has moved things around and responded quickly in terms of the management of the crisis . As you rightly highlight, it is a huge humanitarian crisis and a huge geopolitical crisis. I t is definitely dominating the FCDO , and that is very clear in the engagements we have had with it. Our worry is less the attention on Ukraine, which is right and proper , but that it crowds out other, equally difficult crises where people are in as much or more need around the world. That is our concern on that.

As I mentioned, the Ukraine crisis is fairly new , and in some ways Afghanistan might be a better example to look at because we have had a bit more time to look at it. There are definite ly some positives about the way the FCDO worked the re, but also some challenges around that in terms of how the whole - of - government approach operated . Learning the lessons from Afghanistan to feed into the Ukraine crisis response would be very helpful.

To take the question into a wider context, Stephanie mentioned that aid programmes are long-term projects, by and large, and require sustained effort, but that the FCDO is focused on the here and now, short-term issues and crises. Of course , one always has to respond to crises, but one would also hope that the UK had a foreign policy that took a rather longer - term view. To that extent, would you say that the criticism is rather less about the merger than about the fact that the Foreign Office h as not , in your opinion, been taking such a long - term strategic view and , indeed, maybe the G overnment have not been taking such a long - term strategic view?

Yes, t hat is probably fair. Again, we will see a bit more when the international development strategy comes out, but the FCDO could have development at its heart; i t could be very focused on the long term as well as the short term. We have not seen much of that yet. Obviously, Ukraine and Afghanistan have been huge crises and will have dominated attention. I suppose that the proof of the pudding will be how money gets allocated, what the priorities are and whether there is that long - term strategic investment in conflict prevention , for example, which will prevent some of these crises becoming so bad in future. Can the FCDO manage both of those challenges?

The biggest geopolitical crisis in generations in Ukraine, hundreds of other crises around the world, climate change, a global pandemic : there is a lot on the FCDO ’ s plate. It will be really interesting to see h ow it manages that tension between focusing on what is in the news right now , what challenges the UK ’ s own security and national interest s , and that longer - term focus on reducing inequality and poverty and preventing conflict . It certainly will not be easy. We are already seeing difficult choices being made about where the focus and the money go.

Q8 Lord Campbell of Pittenweem : I declare an interest as an ambassador for the charity Halo. As I think you know, it is responsible for mine clearance and, increasingly, improvised explosive devices. At the moment it is operating in Afghanistan with the acceptance of the Taliban. I am trying to avoid special pleading, but you raised the question of how priorities are to be identified and implemented. As it happens, the funding for Halo in Afghanistan comes from Germany and the U nited S tates . Do you think the new structure is sufficiently flexible to allow for the change of priorities and emphasis, or do you think that changes of priorities and emphasis will always be driven by what is current, such as Ukraine or, previously, Afghanistan?

That is a great question and I think it remains to be seen. That is the challenge of the merger, is it not? Previously there was a separate department that was able to focus on the longer - term picture and was not pulled too much into immediate foreign policy priorities. There are c hallenges around having separate departments . DfID had the expertise to respond to humanitarian crises around the world, and did it very well. The merger will challenge the ability to flex and respond to different priorities as they come up . The merger is not really complete yet . There are different systems in place and lots of movement of people . Hopefully there will be that ability to flex to different priorities.

I t is also important that some of th e long er- term priorities stay the same. The FCDO is only 18 months old but we have already had several different sets of priorities during those 18 months. We would not want to see continu ally changing sets of priorities. Obviously, the real world happens and throws up new priorities , but t he ability to maintain that long er- term focus will be a real challenge .

Lord Campbell of Pittenweem : I had not realised that James Cleverly has such a wide range of responsibilities. From any dealings I have had with him, I know him as conscientious and d etermined to do his best, but it is quite difficult to imagine someone given that range of responsibilities being confident that in every respect they will be able to fulfil all th e se obligations .

Q9 Stephanie Draper mentioned that in the old days DfID was accountable; I wondered whether she meant that the FCDO is not accountable. I go back to the days when Lynda Chalker was in charge of international development as part of the Foreign Office, with Douglas Hurd as Foreign Secretary. It worked superbly well and an enormous amount of work was done. I remember, because afterwards I was in the department , that DfID grew not just because of the 0 .7% aid budget. With t he buildings in P alace St reet, the number of people who worked there and the amount of money it had—I was trying to look up what the DfID budget was— it did fantastic things, but there was a huge amount of waste . No body seems to mention how much the merger has saved the taxpayer but not on projects ; t he projects can still go on and be done. It is a matter of whether there is a really good Df ID M inister within the Foreign Office, as we had with Lynda Chalker.

On the point about accountability and transparency, according to the independent watchdogs and the IATI transparency system, t he long and short of it was that Df ID always scored very well in the accountability and transparency of its ODA spending, and the Foreign Office did not. Those two have now come together. We hope that we will tak e forward the high standard that Df ID used to have, but we have not yet seen that, partly because of all these difficult decisions and p artly , probably , because in the Foreign Office there was less of a culture of transparency , for understandable reasons. We really hope to see that improve over time.

You talked about projects and waste. That too will be one of the challenges because, again , Df ID was a world leader in development and very well respected , with generally excellent projects that were viewed and independently evaluated very well . It was one of the most scrutinised government departments in the UK, so those mechanisms to ensure quality were there and were strong , and generally Df ID performed very well. The DfID projects were considered very good value for money. Foreign Office projects that used overseas development assistance funding scored less well in value for money and reaching those most in need, so again there is the cultural challenge of how you bring up to the previous standards the work of the whole FCDO. That is another ongoing challenge.
Q10 I was L y nda Chalker ’ s opposite number, and I recall the skill, with political clout, with which she solved the problem of Uganda by building bridges with President Museveni after his coup.

My question is simply this. Obviously it is difficult to disentangle the effect of the merger and the cuts. We know that the aid community is still totally hostile to the cuts. Has the attitude to the merger been reduced as a result of practi c e?

I think we are waiting to see a little bit , particularly with the international development strategy. We were promised this strategy some time ago. It has been delayed. We have had several different Foreign Secretaries , who have wanted to put their own stamp on it. As I said , we have had improved engagement recently with the FCDO , so that is good signal , b ut the legacy of the aid cuts has obviously stung the sector . W e are waiting to see what the Government ’ s priorities and the role of delivery partners are in helping to deliver the UK ’ s priorities.

A lot will become clearer for us o nce we see the development strategy and see whether development genuinely will be at the heart of the FCDO or not. We have mentioned already some of the signs that that will be a challenge, and that is a worry for us. T he sector awaits reassurance that development will be a key part of the development, defence and diplomacy portfolio of the UK Government, as per the integrated review.

As people said earlier, there is not necessarily a problem with the merger itself as a structural thing, provided that we feel the reassurance that it is a genuine merger of two partners and that development is not lost within it.

I th a nk you for your evidence this morning, and for Stephanie Draper ’ s, who was with us for the first half-hour of the session. You have given us an extremely good grounding for our next session. We will reflect very carefully on the main themes that you have brought forward. I kept hearing issues about a reduction in transparency in the way the G overnment may be operating in its relations with the development sector, which is a concern. Like you, we look forward to seeing the NAO report tomorrow and examining its implications.

Witnesses

I : David Rutley MP, Minister for Welfare Delivery at Department for Work and Pensions ; Mims Davies MP, Minister for Employment at Department for Work and Pensions ; Neil Couling, Director General, Change Group at Department for Work and Pensions ; and Donna Ward, Director for Poverty, Family and Disadvantage at Department for Work and Pensions .
Written evidence from witnesses:
Department for Work and Pensions (UCC0015)
Examination of W itnesses
Witnesses: David Rutley, Mims Davies , Neil Couling and Donna Ward .

Q99 A warm welcome , everybody , to this meeting of the Work and Pensions Select Committee in our inquiry on the support for the costs of childcare. This is the final evidence session in this inquiry. We a re delighted to welcome the two Ministers and their team this morning . Thank you both for being here. David, do you want to start by introducing yourself, and Mim s , do the same?

Absolutely. I am the Minister for Welfare Delivery. Mims can introduce herself , but she needs no introduction. Neil Couling is the SRO for Universal Credit , but also the D irector G eneral for the Change Group. Donna Ward, to Mims ’ s left, is D irector for Poverty, Family and Disadvantage and knows a lot about childcare, so it is good to have her here as well.
Good morning, everybody. I am the Member of Parliament for Mid Sussex and I have had the pleasure of being the Employment Minister for nearly three years, which is quite surprising.

Q100 Well done. Yes, thank you. We are very pleased to see you all here . We have lots of questions that we would like to ask you about this subject and I will start. You are probably aware that we have heard quite a lot of criticism in our inquiry of the effectiveness of the current arrangements for supporting the costs of childcare. Can one of you give us an assessment of the effectiveness of childcare support in Universal Credit , including its cost effectiveness? What is the Government ’ s view on this? We know that Ministers have resisted the idea of a review of the childcare system . Why is that? Do you recognise that we do need some changes in this area?

I will start. Thanks again for the invitation . This is an important subject . A s you can see , we have two Ministers here and two very senior officials to help us answer the questions from the Committee.

In terms of cost - effectiveness, it is obviously very difficult to attribute directly the labour market progression that is linked specifically to Universal Credit childcare. However , t hat also needs to be seen in context of the wider support that we are providing across Universal Credit , which is £41 billion in 2021-22. It is worth reminding ourselves —I am sure that t he Committee is aware of this—that the UC childcare cost element is just one part of a comprehensive offer of childcare, including the free childcare that is available through DfE funding in England and other offers around tax - free childcare , and so forth.

What I would say is that as we look at the impact that this is having and the outcomes that we want to drive , p articularly with Universal Credit , it is about trying to help people overcome barriers into work. If we look at what is going on with female employment rates particularly, which are absolutely critical, that is currently at 72.2%, which is a 13.7 percentage point increase on 2010. In terms of lo ne parents, the employment rate is 66.7%, which is an 11.6 percentage point increase on 2010. If we add those factors in, we can see that the direct impact that that is going to have on people and their opportunities to work is very real and clear. Directly attributing it to the Universal Credit childcare element specifically is quite difficult. I am sure Mims can say more on the labour market effect.

In terms of a review, I am sure we will come on to this later on , but there is now an IMG — inter ministerial group — on family, which is chaired by the Secretary of State for Education. It is looking at childcare across G overnment. As for w hether it is as specific as the formal review that you are referring to, Chair , I can assure the Committee that this is being looked at in the round through an IMG.
Q101 Has that been set up very recently?
It has, yes.
Q102 Chair : In response to what?

In response to the Government wanting to do more to understand the impact of their policy and what they can do to support families. The childcare dimension is a subject that is at the top of the list.
What is the timescale for that group to review—
It is an ongoing IMG and it has its own agenda , which the Education Secretary is driving forward.

Q103 Your description of it acknowledges that it is a very complicated landscape at the moment. There are lots of different schemes trying to work out what is the right thing for people to do and, as you say, the cost - effectiveness of it all is quite difficult. Do you accept that?

It is an offer across childcare that involves several elements. We are working very hard to make sure that our work coaches can help explain clearly what offer might be most effective to the claimant in the space that we work in. I was at Thornaby Jobcentre last week—again , we will talk about the promotion activity that we are doing in due course , I am sure —and it was great to see how, unprompted, childcare was very prominent in the jobcentre. When I spoke to them about this particular subject and about coming to see the Committee this week, they were very clear that they were given training and support.

Yes, we do need to do more to help simplify this and to communicate the offers , and I am sure that we will come on to that as well. Mims may want to say more about the labour market aspects and what goes on in terms of helping to clarify this for our claimants.

I was at Crawley Jobcentre yesterday , our new site, working with Gatwick Airport and with the supply chain specifically in and around Crawley , where there are around 5,000 jobs available in the vicinity. I ha ve never met a more diverse group of employers who were willing and able to flex hours around claimants and opportunities. It was quite staggering .

I do not know how many jobcentres the Committee has been to see recently. Selaine, you were w ith your jobcentre over the recess. I do not know how much evidence you have taken directly from work coaches, but it is very rare that I hear childcare is the single issue that is stopping people progressing. It is very often transport, wider caring issues, training or confidence. There are always other things going on and we are looking at the barriers that are stopping our claimants from progressing . Childcare is very rare, in my experience, as a single issue that is stopping people from moving forward.

Our work coaches are absolutely brilliant at delving into what is going on in a claimant ’ s life that is holding them back. They have those tailored one-to-one conversations and i f childcare or the cost is a barrier, they will d rill into that before people are looking to go into work. Quite often, lone parents , particularly, or people in different situations are not ready to go straight into work. They will need the Flexible Support Fund . T hey will need help not just for childcare for going into work , but for training, for confidence, for getting the experience of going back into work, which our work coaches are very good at.

In fact, the Secretary of State and I have a monthly conversation with work coaches up and down the land about what is going on and what is holding claimants back or what is frustrating our work coaches on the ground and how we can fix it. One of the largest interventions of those conversations is being able to use the Flexible Support Fund for people in the lighter-touch category sooner and more widely. That was exactly because work coaches felt, particularly for lone parents and people with caring responsibilities, that that could help them progress sooner. Therefore it is not something that comes through to me, as Employment Minister, as a singular issue that is holding people back.

Explaining the bread th of support t here is very important. Obviously we have our work coaches doing that up and down the land individually with people and we have good childcare explainer s and other things through our DWP comms. I was at the Emirates at a job fair recently , focus ed on Kickstart . I met a 21 - year-old girl who was taken on by a fantastic restaurant company. She was a lone parent at 21. She knew after that jobs fair and working with us that the employer was incredibly flexible around what she could do—that was a massive eye-opener for her—and , secondly , that the Flexible Support Fund and help with childcare and those costs was available for her.

A lot of people need to know that on the ground it is a lot easier than you think. I would love for you to chat to our work coaches and get out on the ground to see whether this is really what is holding claimants back. We saw in the in-work progression report, which we are currently putting our response to, it is much wider. It is transport ; it is confidence. There are other things that are holding people back. Quite often , it is that mix of things.

Q104 There are circumstances in which, if people increase their hours, by the time they have paid for the extra childcare they are worse off as a result of working more. It should not be like that, should it?

No, it should not, but many of us — I was a single working mum — have been at the point where you are wondering what it is all about and how you are progressing. It is something that happens whether you are a Universal Credit claimant or not. Sometimes you are literally paddling to continue. I am not saying that that is acceptable , I am saying that that is part of the challenge of being a working parent and how you manage that. Donna, I will turn to you there.

I can come in on some of the calculations that have been offered to the Committee on the marginal returns . It is true that once you go beyond the childcare cap and you are paying for childcare yourself, the marginal return is quite low. However, the thing that we focus on with claimants is the better-off calculation. What is the difference between working versus not working or working 30 hours versus 15 hours? Those are the sorts of choices that people are making. Taking everything together, the work allowance, the £600-odd that you already get fro m childcare support and so on, it looks a lot better than just looking at your last marginal hour. Wherever you put the childcare cap, you would get the problem that once you go over the cap , the marginal hour looks bad at that point , but it is the better-off calculation , taking everything together.
Can I say something on how we know whether the childcare market is successful generally?
We will come back to that , if we may , in response to later questions .

Q105 I would like to know why only 6% of those claiming the child element of Universal Credit are also claiming the childcare element. However, we are not even sure about that 6%, are we ? T hat figure is not robust. We are told that t he Department has its own way of estimating, its own methodology, but that is not sufficiently robust to be used in official statistics. That begs the question : do we know enough about our clients, about the claimants? Have you sufficient ambition to find out more about them and how changes in policy will therefore have an impact on them? Have you look ed at the cost-benefit analysis of finding out more about them?

A typically incisive question fro m Sir Desmond, and thank you for it. We have tried to explain in the correspondence prior to this hearing that it is difficult for us currently to measure the true take-up rate. It is partly about the denominator and what is included. The 6% includes people who are not in work, those who are not eligible, so it is low at 6%. In te rms of our ambition to get more information to become more incisive, we are conducting further analysis. I can commit to the Chair and to you, Sir De s mond, that we will be publishing that and it will produce an estimate of in - work Universal Credit claims in receipt of the childcare element . It will show a range of characteristics as well , the age of the youngest child and so forth. O bviously , we will get the data to you in due course.

The analysis that we are working on show s that over 50% of working families on Universal Credit have school-aged children . That means that those parents are not so much in need of childcare as perhaps one might think. For those with children of pre - school age , DfE ’ s free entitlements are sometimes sufficient, particularly since many Universal Credit claimants are part time.

It is also clear fro m DfE ’ s research that lower- income families are more likely to use more informal types of childcare to provide the support. That is about not just affordability, but flexibility — the point that Mims was making earlier on about some of the uncertainty that parents are facing. They are the factors that have come out. As I have said though, we will be publishing that analysis as soon as possible and we w ill forward it to the Committee. Also , Sir Desmond, we are ambitious to increase the take-up rate too. There is a lot of work that we will be doing to significantly improve that and the Committee will hear more about that — unfortunately not today , but there is activity in terms of both clarifying the data and driving the take-up rate.

Q106 Notwithstanding the conversations to be had with work coaches, the conversations we have been having with the claimants show that they are having a g reat deal of difficulty meeting the up - front costs of childcare. Beyond the measures that you have already taken, is there any more that we can expect from you to address this issue and the extent —if we are even aware of it, knowing sufficient ly about our clients —to w hich it is an impediment to people taking on work or taking on more work?

We know that the up - front costs, fro m the evidence that you have received, can create some cash - flow issues. We sympathise with that. That is in part the operating model that the childcare providers have , in the sense that they want payment in advance rather than in arrears . Neil will have a clear view on this, having helped to design Universal Credit in the first place.

One of the fundamental design principles of Universal Credit is that we want to understand people ’ s actual costs and actual hours worked, their earnings, to then work out a whole payment — not just the standard element b ut the other elements , including the childcare element. Of course , to help with that up - front piece and the barriers is the Flexible Support Fund. W e have the design principle of Universal Credit that is more generous than the Working Tax Credit by some distance and then we have the Flexible Support Fund to try to help up front. Neil , is there anything you want to say about the design of Universal Credit at this stage?

Yes, briefly. The one bi t of advice I got fro m Steve Lamey, who was running Benefits and Credits in HMRC back in 2010 , was , “D on ’ t pay childcare costs in advance ; pay them in arrears ” . HMRC has a big problem in tax credits w ith fraud with childcare. I f we were paying in advance and had the same level of fraud th at tax credit s have in Universal Credit , it would have cost £170 million last year. In fact, the amount we lost to fraud in childcare was only £1 million by paying it in arrears. As t he Minister says, that does give some cash-flow issues and that part of the market is adjusting, I am certain, to the fact that we pay in arrears rather than in advance like tax credits . But if we went back to paying it in advance, first , I do not know how you would do it with the design of Universal Credit —that is another question —and s econdly , you would create a fraud problem.
In terms of the up - front piece, Mims, you may want to say something about the Flexible Support Fund, because that helps pay the first month for many people.

In fact , it can be slightly further on. The discretion is up to the work coach. As Donna inferred about the better-off calculations in terms of being in work , we want people to take a job, progress and stay in work. We do not want to set them up to fail, hence we want the Flexible Support Fund, where it is supporting childcare costs, to work for them and for them to spring forward from that point.

Sir Desmond, you asked a wider question that I would be keen to address about understanding our claimants ’ needs , why they are stuck and how we can help them further. Just this month , the in-work progression work will be rolling out. It has existed since May 2021 in South Yorkshire, covering Doncaster, Sheffield and Barnsley. This is working one - to - one with work coaches. We are going to have 37 progression champions across the piece to spearhead working with partners — including employers and skills providers — to identify the opportunities for those lower-paid claimants to help them move into better paid work, to get more confidence, help make ends meet and move fro m that stuck cohort.

The evidence that we have learn ed from South Yorkshire is being rolled out f ro m this month. That is part of the in-work progression report response. As I said earlier, childcare was one element there — for sure — confidence was massive , and transport and accessibility very often was a challenge. That again is where the Flexible Support Fund can help people.

For example, in the south-west, there are schemes like Wheels to Work, which puts on buses and support to get people to particular factory work or other areas where hours or public transport does not work , so they can use that or a bus fare or whatever through the Flexible Support Fund. We are looking at any barrier that is holding people back from getting into their first job — any job — and then that better job and that career through in-work progression , and we are l ooking at all of this in the round , as David described.

Q107 On that specific point, my understanding is that you cannot have access to the Flexible Support Fund if you have earn ed more than £2,600 or something in the previous six months. If it is a progression point , then the Flexible Support Fund probably cannot help. Is that right?

No, it is not. There was a slight confusion in the evidence of one of your previous witnesses, which I will have a go at trying to explain. That witness was talking about earnings limits of £2,600 in six months , or £ 3,6 00. That is the qualifying condition for a budgeting loan, which can be used as well in the system to help people with the initial costs of childcare or perhaps more likely th e costs in the summer or something where childcare costs may go up. It was a confusion , I think, between the rules for budgeting loans rather than the Flexible Support Fund that does not have a n earnings rule in it.
That is helpful ; thank you.

Apologies for lateness — childcare problems. I want to make a quick point on the up - front costs. Minister, you mentioned that it ca u ses a cash-flow problem. It ca u ses a cash - flow problem every single term. I will just make this point and I am not going to make you talk again on this . It is the one aspect of this that is undermining the whole policy, the generosity of the policy and what you are trying to achieve, because you have parents who are scrabbling around and really struggling. This is the evidence not just from the witnesses we have heard from, but from my own constituents. The very nature of that constant fight and constant batt le and borrowing and then not being able to pay it back is a real issue for this policy .

Q108 We are sticking with the Flexible Support Fund that we heard about earlier . If we accept that one of the aims of Universal Credit is to get people into work — that is what you are very focused on — why do you think so few work coaches and parents have heard about the Flexible Support Fund , and what exactly are you doing to change that?

I will take that one. We have a regular meeting each Wednesday across DWP for training and support and awareness. I am not going to deny that , as a work coach , you have a bloomin g bi g workload and huge knowledge base. There is no doubt that we ask a lot from our work coaches in terms of their understanding. That is why we have special points of contact. Very often , those are the people who process Flexible Support Fund claims. You have the mother hens, as they are described by our Secretary of State sometimes , in terms of being the all-seeing eyes i n jobcentres who can help particularly newer work coaches taking on new understanding.

One thing that the Secretary of State and I have been very keen to do with the Flexible Support Fund is increase that knowledge and understand ing and that discretion piece . As y ou mentioned , Steve, it is about making sure that people use it on the ground to unlock barriers for people, whether that is a haircut, a new suit, the first month ’ s bus fare or support with childcare , so that our work coaches are confident ly bringing it forward and using it. If I am honest , I have heard that sometimes the perception is, “W e need to be careful about that fund. We need to look after it, we never know who might need it”. I have been o f the other mind set that—
Q109 It has been underspent for 11 years.

Absolutely. In my mind , it is completely the opposite. If there is a barrier, particularly for younger people through the Kicks tart scheme — having the right work clothes, bus far e , haircut , anything they have needed — the Flexible Support Fund has been the way of unlocking that barrier. The Flexible Support Fund is not solely for childcare ; it is for all of the things that I have just described, including transport. This is about making sure that work coaches , jobcentres and local leadership feel confident that they are spending the money the right way and that we , as Ministers in the Department , are going to back them up because they are spending it to unlock those barriers.
Q110 Are you monitoring, Minister, whether or not these ambitions of yours are being translated into action?
Yes, there is the management around cascading the message s , which I started with, and trying to look at how it is spent. Each area, each community, each claimant will be different.

Q111 I want to understand this. I am not sure how you have been monitoring it and what sorts of things you are monitoring. Is it how many people get a new suit , how many people get help with childcare or how many people g et help with travel in the first weeks? Do you have hard indicators where we can see what the pro gr ess is? As I say, if it has been underspent every year for 11 years, I would expect the underspend to be reducing as well. That would be evidence of the success of your efforts , would it not?
We got additional Flexible Support Fund through the Plan for Jobs, through the Chancellor, to help.
Q112 Why would you need more if you could not spend what you had?

We had, for example, funding for 250,000 Kickstart places. We have fulfilled over 160,000, but we had a much l ower unemployment gap to fil l . Therefore we have not needed to spend it. Nobody here at DWP is frivolous and I would not expect anybody at any level, particularly on the g round, to feel, “Hey, it ’ s there, let ’ s just go and spend it”. I think that our work coaches use their discretion. Th ey tailor the needs of the claimant. We do have breakdowns in terms of categories — removing barriers, training, childcare , partnerships and other s . I have been very keen as well to use it more widely to support people who are in self-employment or to get set up in self-employment.
Q113 This monitoring that you are doing that shows the progress you are making — is that something the Committee could see?
The Minister wrote to the Committee with the figures for 2021 on 30 December 2021.
We shared it, yes.
Q114 Does that break down what I have been asking : how much you are spending on childcare ; how many people have new suits ? Does it tell me that?
I t breaks it down by category and by geography.
Q115 What does it tell me, Neil? That would be helpful. I am sorry .
